signal.title: envoy: propagate Kubernetes backend locality into generated EDS resources
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? yes. Enabling: ```yaml envoy: nodeLocality: enabled: true ``` does not currently appear to enable end-to-end Envoy zone-aware routing for Kubernetes Service backends synchronized by OSS Cilium. I verified this in: - [`v1.20.1`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/tree/v1.20.1) - [`v1.21.0-pre.0`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/tree/v1.21.0-pre.0) - current [`main`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/commit/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a) The local Envoy can learn its own zone, but Envoy is still missing two required pieces of locality information: 1. `/cilium-locality-cluster` is configured as the originating cluster, but OSS Cilium does not appear to publish an EDS `ClusterLoadAssignment` containing the Cilium Envoy instances grouped by zone. 2. Cilium-generated service EDS assignments put every Kubernetes backend into one `LocalityLbEndpoints` without setting `locality.zone`. Without those distributions, Envoy cannot apply its documented best-effort zone-aware routing algorithm. This is useful in multi-AZ production clusters because local-zone preference can reduce cross-AZ latency and transfer costs while providing more predictable failure-domain behavior. #### Existing implementation PR [#44696](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44696) added the initial locality infrastructure: - `envoy.nodeLocality.enabled`, defaulting to `false` - lookup of `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` - passing the resolved zone to standalone Envoy through `--service-zone` - population of `node.locality.zone` for embedded Envoy - `cluster_manager.local_cluster_name: /cilium-locality-cluster` - an EDS cluster definition for `/cilium-locality-cluster` - startup failure when the local zone cannot be resolved PR [#45568](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/45568) exported `LocalityClusterName`. The source comment says: > Keep the constant public to make it accessible in downstream repos. The current bootstrap implementation is here: - [standalone Envoy bootstrap](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/install/kubernetes/cilium/files/cilium-envoy/configmap/bootstrap-config.yaml#L285-L305) - [embedded Envoy bootstrap](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/envoy/locality.go#L20-L65) I could not find production code in OSS Cilium that publishes a `ClusterLoadAssignment` for `/cilium-locality-cluster`. The only assignment I found is created manually by [`TestEnvoyAdsLocalityClusterEndpointsACK`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/envoy/standalone_envoy_test.go#L1516-L1625). That verifies that Envoy accepts a caller-supplied assignment, not that Cilium generates one automatically. #### Current service EDS behavior The shared CEC backend processor retrieves the Kubernetes Service backends and calls `computeLoadAssignments()`. In `v1.20.1`, `v1.21.0-pre.0`, and current `main`, the function creates one endpoint group: ```go endpoints := []*envoy_config_endpoint.LocalityLbEndpoints{ { LbEndpoints: lbEndpoints, }, } ``` It does not set `Locality`. Permanent references: - [`v1.20.1`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/7d68cfb394f2960e10aa72e76d0d51e66c1b2ebc/pkg/ciliumenvoyconfig/controller.go#L405-L543) - [`v1.21.0-pre.0`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/e864986222d3b2d9fad0fc508cb875687e718f96/pkg/ciliumenvoyconfig/controller.go#L405-L543) - [`main`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/ciliumenvoyconfig/controller.go#L405-L543) The backend data model already contains `NodeName` and `Zone`, and the EndpointSlice reflector populates them: - [`loadbalancer.Backend`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/loadbalancer/backend.go#L27-L123) - [EndpointSlice zone parsing](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/k8s/endpoints.go#L301-L333) - [backend zone propagation](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/6fd7b3f536d6da5ce8cdb48019ca50c3d52caf0a/pkg/loadbalancer/reflectors/endpoints/endpoints.go#L168-L180) For normal EndpointSlice-derived backends, the controller appears to be discarding zone information that is already available. #### This is separate from eBPF Service Topology This request is not about: ```yaml loadBalancer: serviceTopology: true ``` That setting, EndpointSlice topology hints, and `trafficDistribution` affect backend selection in the eBPF and kube-proxy-replacement Service datapath. They do not populate locality in Envoy EDS resources after traffic has been redirected through Cilium's L7 proxy. #### Confirmed affected paths The shared backend-sync controller is used by: - `CiliumEnvoyConfig` and `CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig` `services` - `CiliumEnvoyConfig` and `CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig` `backendServices` - `service.cilium.io/lb-l7: enabled` - Cilium Ingress-generated backend clusters - Gateway API HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, and TLS passthrough configurations that generate a CEC - GAMMA HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute configurations that generate a CEC Pure L4 Gateway paths that do not generate a CEC are not included here. #### Envoy requirements Envoy's documentation requires more than the originating proxy's zone. Zone-aware routing also needs: - an EDS originating cluster selected through `local_cluster_name` - the originating cluster's host distribution by zone - upstream EDS endpoints grouped by locality - a supported load-balancing policy - enough upstream hosts - healthy originating and upstream clusters outside panic mode - priority `P=0` References: - [Envoy configuration requirements](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/faq/configuration/zone_aware_routing) - [zone-aware routing behavior](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/zone_aware) - [runtime defaults](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/upstream/cluster_manager/cluster_runtime) - [panic-mode behavior](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/panic_threshold) The default minimum upstream cluster size is six, and the default panic threshold is 50 percent. Cilium's generated L7 Service configuration supports `ROUND_ROBIN`, `LEAST_REQUEST`, and `RANDOM`, which support locality-aware routing. #### Related work Open PR [#47335](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47335) overlaps the upstream EDS portion of this request. At its current head, it only groups endpoints by zone when `Backend.Zone.ForZones` is populated: - [PR #47335 implementation](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/45416a86be1a5823a44f6907302aea299f6245fd/pkg/ciliumenvoyconfig/controller.go#L493-L554) It does not currently: - populate `/cilium-locality-cluster` - connect the behavior to `envoy.nodeLocality.enabled` - emit locality when physical backend zones exist without topology hints - test actual multi-zone Envoy routing and fallback `ForZones` describes where Kubernetes recommends consuming an endpoint. `Backend.Zone.Zone` describes where the endpoint is physically located. Those values are related but not equivalent. I searched open and closed issues, PRs, and discussions and did not find an exact issue tracking the complete behavior. Issues [#40883](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/40883), [#37930](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/37930), and [#18710](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/18710) concern the eBPF Service topology path. [#30235](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/30235) proposed a broader xDS adapter. [#27935](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/27935) concerns an unrelated L7 Service port failure. #### Validation The source findings were also confirmed at runtime in a multi-zone cluster: - EKS with Kubernetes v1.36 - 11 nodes across `ca-central-1a` and `ca-central-1b`, with every node labeled using `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` - Cilium v1.20.1 installed through Helm, with kube-proxy replacement, ENI IPAM, native routing, WireGuard, and Gateway API enabled - the dedicated `cilium-envoy` DaemonSet - `envoy.nodeLocality.enabled=true` The workload, namespace, Gateway, Service, and pod names and the endpoint IP addresses below have been replaced with consistent placeholders. The zones, counts, commands, and observed behavior are unchanged. On a proxy running in `ca-central-1b`, standalone Envoy receives the local zone through `--service-zone`: ```console $ cilium-dbg envoy admin serverinfo | jq '.command_line_options.service_zone' "ca-central-1b" ``` The generated bootstrap also sets the local cluster name. `node.locality` is null in this standalone bootstrap dump because the process receives its zone through the command line: ```console $ cilium-dbg envoy admin config | jq '.configs[] | select(."@type" | contains("Bootstrap")) | .bootstrap | {node_locality: .node.locality, local_cluster_name: .cluster_manager.local_cluster_name}' { "node_locality": null, "local_cluster_name": "/cilium-locality-cluster" } ``` The two missing EDS inputs are visible on that same proxy. First, `/cilium-locality-cluster` is configured, but it has no host assignment: ```console $ cilium-dbg envoy admin clusters | grep -cE '^/cilium-locality-cluster::[0-9]' 0 ``` Second, every host in a Gateway-API-generated backend cluster has an empty zone and sub-zone: ```console $ cilium-dbg envoy admin clusters | grep 'example-backend.*:192\.0\.2\.' | grep -E 'zone' cilium-gateway/cilium-gateway-example-gateway/example-app:example-backend:8080::192.0.2.10:8080::zone:: cilium-gateway/cilium-gateway-example-gateway/example-app:example-backend:8080::192.0.2.10:8080::sub_zone:: cilium-gateway/cilium-gateway-example-gateway/example-app:example-backend:8080::192.0.2.20:8080::zone:: cilium-gateway/cilium-gateway-example-gateway/example-app:example-backend:8080::192.0.2.20:8080::sub_zone:: ``` The EndpointSlice for the same Service contains the physical zone for both endpoints: ```console $ kubectl get endpointslices -n example-app -l kubernetes.io/service-name=example-backend -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].endpoints[*]}{.addresses[0]}{@.zone} {end}' 192.0.2.10@ca-central-1a 192.0.2.20@ca-central-1b ``` For contrast, the eBPF Service datapath on the same cluster consumes the topology data correctly with `loadBalancer.serviceTopology=true` and `trafficDistribution` set on the Service. The per-node BPF map on the `ca-central-1b` node contained only the `ca-central-1b` backend. The zone data exists end to end and is lost only on the Envoy backend synchronization path. While live traffic was flowing through the Gateway, all exposed `envoy_cluster_lb_zone_*` and `envoy_cluster_lb_local_cluster_not_ok` counters remained `0` across 330 zone-routing stat series. This is consistent with the missing locality data, but it is not used here as standalone proof: this example cluster has two backends and therefore does not meet Envoy's default minimum cluster size of six hosts. The direct config evidence above does not depend on that threshold. The existing backend-sync fixture also expects [one locality-less endpoint group](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/e864986222d3b2d9fad0fc508cb875687e718f96/pkg/ciliumenvoyconfig/testdata/backendservices.txtar#L288-L345). ### Describe the feature you'd like When `envoy.nodeLocality.enabled=true`, Cilium should provide all locality information required by Envoy's zone-aware algorithm. Generated service EDS resources should look roughly like: ```yaml endpoints: - locality: zone: ca-central-1a lb_endpoints: - endpoint: ... - locality: zone: ca-central-1b lb_endpoints: - endpoint: ... ``` The `/cilium-locality-cluster` assignment should also describe the distribution of the relevant Cilium Envoy instances by zone. When healthy local-zone capacity exists and Envoy's prerequisites are satisfied, Envoy should prefer it according to its documented best-effort algorithm. When no healthy local-zone backend exists, requests should fall back to healthy remote-zone backends, subject to Envoy's documented panic-mode behavior. #### Documentation concern The current Helm documentation correctly says that Cilium resolves the local Node zone and passes it to standalone Envoy through `--service-zone`. However, the agent flag and release-note wording can reasonably be interpreted as enabling end-to-end zone-aware routing. Until the implementation is complete, the documentation should state that the option only supplies local Envoy metadata and bootstrap infrastructure. It does not currently make Cilium-generated upstream service clusters zone-aware without another control plane supplying the missing EDS resources. #### Acceptance criteria - Cilium-generated EDS resources group resolved Kubernetes backends by zone - Envoy config dump shows locality for the originating proxy and upstream Service endpoints - `/cilium-locality-cluster` receives a usable zonal EDS assignment - a valid multi-zone test demonstrates best-effort local-zone preference - traffic falls back to healthy remote-zone backends when local backends are unavailable - behavior for missing backend locality is deterministic and documented - embedded Envoy and standalone `cilium-envoy` are supported - every confirmed generated L7 path using the shared controller is tested - documentation explains prerequisites, limitations, panic behavior, minimum cluster size, and the distinction from eBPF Service Topology ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/envoy @cilium/sig-servicemesh ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution The exact implementation is for maintainers to decide, but likely work includes: 1. use the existing `Backend.Zone.Zone` value 2. optionally resolve `Backend.NodeName` when EndpointSlice locality is missing 3. group Service backends deterministically by zone 4. populate `envoy.config.core.v3.Locality` 5. keep physical endpoint locality separate from `ForZones` topology hints 6. define deterministic behavior for unresolved zones 7. populate `/cilium-locality-cluster` in OSS Cilium 8. support embedded and standalone Envoy 9. add unit and multi-node integration tests

signal.title: preferredIPv6Address() (IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING) ignores deprecated/public-vs-private status, unlike the newer NodeAddress table logic
signal.text: ## Title `preferredIPv6Address()` (IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING) ignores deprecated/public-vs-private status, unlike the newer NodeAddress table logic ## Summary On a node whose direct-routing device carries **two** global-scope IPv6 addresses — a stable ULA and a deprecated (`preferred_lft 0`) SLAAC/GUA address learned via RA — `IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING` (baked into `node_config.h` at agent startup, used by the eBPF datapath for NodePort/LoadBalancer SNAT when forwarding to a non-local backend) can end up set to the **deprecated GUA** instead of the ULA, depending purely on which address the kernel happens to enumerate first. Traffic that gets SNAT'd to that address never receives a reply, since nothing in the surrounding network expects return traffic addressed to it. This reproduces deterministically per-node (not per-packet) — of 4 otherwise-identical nodes in our cluster, 3 have the wrong address baked in and 1 has the correct one, and it's been stable across a full agent restart on the affected nodes (confirmed the fresh agent re-read the same wrong address). ## Environment - Cilium 1.20.1, `kubeProxyReplacement: true`, `Masquerading: IPTables [IPv4: Enabled, IPv6: Enabled]` - Talos Linux (kernel 6.18.44), each node's direct-routing device (`ens18`) has: - a statically-assigned ULA, e.g. `fdc1:e344:ba0a:8:10:2:8:81/64` - a SLAAC address from router advertisements, e.g. `2602:47:193:4c08:be24:11ff:fe0a:da37/64`, **already marked `deprecated` by the kernel** (`preferred_lft 0sec`, `valid_lft` still long) - Backend for the affected Service is an external (non-Cilium-managed) address behind a manually authored `EndpointSlice` — i.e. traffic requires SNAT since it's not a local-pod delivery. ## Reproduction ``` $ ip -6 addr show ens18 inet6 2602:47:193:4c08:be24:11ff:fe0a:da37/64 scope global deprecated dynamic mngtmpaddr proto kernel_ra valid_lft 70257sec preferred_lft 0sec inet6 fdc1:e344:ba0a:8:10:2:8:81/64 scope global valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever ``` ``` $ grep ipv6 /run/cilium/state/globals/node_config.h #define IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING { .addr = { 0x26, 0x2, 0x0, 0x47, 0x1, 0x93, 0x4c, 0x8, 0xbe, 0x24, 0x11, 0xff, 0xfe, 0xa, 0xda, 0x37 } } ``` (decodes to `2602:47:193:4c08:be24:11ff:fe0a:da37` — the deprecated address, not the ULA) Confirmed via `cilium endpoint config <host-ep> Debug=Enabled` + `cilium monitor -vv`: the `to-network` forward for a NodePort SYN to the external backend correctly completes conntrack lookup, backend selection, and DNAT — the *only* wrong part is the chosen source address, matching `IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING` exactly. ## Root cause `pkg/datapath/linux/config/config.go`: ```go func preferredIPv6Address(deviceAddresses []tables.DeviceAddress) netip.Addr { var ip netip.Addr for _, addr := range deviceAddresses { if addr.Addr.Is6() { ip = addr.Addr if !ip.IsLinkLocalUnicast() { break } } } return ip } ``` This takes the **first** non-link-local IPv6 address in `deviceAddresses` — whatever order that happens to be in — with no check for `deprecated`/`preferred_lft`, and no public-vs-private preference. The order traces back to raw kernel address-list order, itself a boot-time race between static address configuration and RA-derived SLAAC assignment, so which of the two addresses "wins" is effectively arbitrary per node and stable only until next boot (and not even reliably then). Notably, `pkg/datapath/tables/node_address.go` (the newer `NodeAddress` table, used for BPF masquerade Primary-address selection and `--nodeport-addresses` handling) **already has** explicit public-vs-private preference logic, added specifically for #41866: ```go if addr.Addr.Is6() && !addr.Addr.IsLinkLocalUnicast() { ... if ipv6PublicIndex < 0 && isPublic { ipv6PublicIndex = index } if ipv6PrivateIndex < 0 && !isPublic { ipv6PrivateIndex = index } } ``` `preferredIPv6Address()`/`IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING` never picked up the equivalent treatment — it's a separate, older mechanism operating on the raw `tables.DeviceAddress` list rather than the newer, already-categorized `tables.NodeAddress` table. ## Relation to existing issues - **#36752** ("picks link-local address for IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING") is the same function, but a different, already-fixed edge case: a device with exactly one global address and one link-local, where the pre-fix code picked link-local. Fixed via **#37839**, which is exactly where today's `if !ip.IsLinkLocalUnicast() { break }` check comes from. That fix never addressed disambiguating between **multiple valid global addresses**, which is this issue. - **#41866** (BPF masquerade picks wrong host IP with multiple IPs per interface) is the IPv4 analog for a *different* selection path (`NodeAddress`/masquerade Primary selection), already fixed there. This issue is the equivalent gap in the `IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING`/`preferredIPv6Address` path specifically, which wasn't touched by that fix. ## Suggested fix At minimum, skip addresses with `preferred_lft == 0` (deprecated) in `preferredIPv6Address()` when a non-deprecated alternative exists, mirroring what the kernel's own RFC 6724 address selection already does. Ideally, unify this with the `tables.NodeAddress` public/private-preference logic already present for the masquerade Primary-address and `--nodeport-addresses` paths, so `IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING` doesn't have its own, separately-buggy selection logic at all. ## Workaround found `nodePort.enableDynamicSourceLookup` (CLI: `enable-dynamic-source-lookup-nodeport`, added in 1.20.0 per #44625) bypasses this function entirely for NodePort SNAT by doing a live `BPF_FIB_LOOKUP_SRC` kernel FIB lookup per packet instead of using the static `IPV6_DIRECT_ROUTING` value. Not yet confirmed effective in our environment, but the mechanism (kernel FIB) independently gives the correct answer via `ip -6 route get` on our affected nodes.

Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! BGP peer auto-discovery in defaultGateway mode walks the whole StateDB route table and picks the default route with the lowest metric. The route table is populated from a RT_TABLE_UNSPEC netlink dump, so it holds default routes from every table, not just main — and a default route outside main is not the way off the node. This matters in practice because Cilium installs one itself. With native routing plus any of EnableEnvoyConfig, IPsec, or WireGuard, installFromProxyRoutes* adds default via <cilium_host address> dev cilium_host to table 2005 (RouteTableFromProxy) with no metric, i.e. priority 0. That outranks a real uplink default route, which typically carries a non-zero metric, so auto-discovery hands BGP the cilium_host address as the peer address and the session never comes up. Table 2004 (RouteTableToProxy) similarly holds a local default dev lo; it has no nexthop so it was already skipped, but nothing made that intentional. Restrict selection to unicast routes in the main table, which is where the node's default gateway lives. Non-unicast types (local, blackhole, unreachable, prohibit) do not forward anything either. Test changes: - A new unit case models a node with a metric-1024 main-table default route alongside a metric-0 local default dev lo in table 2004 and a metric-0 default via 10.0.5.160 in table 2005, and asserts the main-table gateway still wins. Existing default routes are built through a small defaultRouteEntry helper so every fixture carries a realistic table and type. - peering-default-gateway.txtar now sets table: 254 / type: 1 on its routes. The fixture previously left both at zero (RT_TABLE_UNSPEC / RTN_UNSPEC), which the kernel never reports for an installed route. release-note Fix BGP `defaultGateway` peer auto-discovery selecting a default route from a non-main routing table, such as the `default via cilium_host` route Cilium installs in the from-proxy table, instead of the node's real default gateway. This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU as peer (on a v1.19.x backport).

signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. - [x] Thanks for contributing! ## Description Inconsistent restored node-map state can associate one node's IPs with multiple IDs. During node deletion, `deallocateIDForNode` selected one matching ID and deallocated only that ID. Secondary forward/reverse mappings, BPF node-map entries, and the corresponding IDs could remain. The deletion path now collects every distinct nonzero ID from deleted-node IPs that have not been reused by another live node, then deallocates each ID exactly once. An ID returns to the pool only after its reverse set is empty, so it remains allocated if a live mapping or a BPF deletion failure remains. A multi-ID mismatch stays diagnostic-only when repair succeeds; actual cleanup failures are still returned. The related allocation/update conflict path can independently leave old IDs unreclaimed. That behavior is known and intentionally out of scope for a focused follow-up. ## Testing ```text go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -run '^TestDeallocateIDsForNode$' -count=1 go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -run '^TestDeallocateIDsForNode$' -count=100 go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -count=1 ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. GitHub Copilot assisted with source analysis, implementation, and test drafting. The final patch was independently reviewed, and all listed checks were run against the exact commit. signal.title: nodediscovery: Make ENI instance facts unoverridable by CNI conf
signal.text: `NetConf.ENI` embeds the whole `awsTypes.ENISpec`, so every `ENISpec` field is CNI-configurable by default. Which of them the mutator actually honors is expressed only as statement position relative to the `GetCustomNetConf` block: `InstanceType`, `AvailabilityZone` and `NodeSubnetID` are assigned after it and are therefore currently unoverridable, but `VpcID` was assigned before it and could be clobbered. Overriding `vpc-id` has exactly two reachable outcomes: set it to the real VPC (a no-op), or set it to any other VPC, in which case the operator selects subnets and security groups in a VPC the instance is not in, `CreateNetworkInterface` would succeed there, but `AttachNetworkInterface` would fail with a cross-VPC attachment error. That happens on allocation attempt, so the misconfiguration would manifest as IP exhaustion rather than as a config error. This PR moves the VpcID assignment down beside its three siblings so IMDS wins, and replace the override with a warning that names both values and states that the CNI conf value is discarded. No currently-working configuration changes behavior, previously-broken ones start working instead of failing obscurely. Note: I discovered this while working on #47974

signal.title: ciliumidentity: include named-port labels in operator-managed identities
signal.text: Fixes: #47214 Pods with named container ports get stuck in ContainerCreating when identityManagementMode=operator. The root cause is a mismatch between how the agent and the operator build the CiliumIdentity key for such pods. The agent includes a gen:io.cilium.k8s.named-ports label in the key, derived from the pod's named container ports. The operator did not, because it called GetCIDKeyFromLabels on the raw k8s label map without ever calling GetPodMetadata, so the named ports were never seen. With different keys, the operator allocates an identity the agent never looks up, and the agent waits for an identity the operator never creates. CNI endpoint creation times out and the pod stays stuck. AIL: 0 ```release-note Fixes a bug where pods with named ports could never be created when operator-managed-identities was enabled. ```

signal.title: Gateway-api: add support for session persistence
signal.text: Add cookie-based Gateway API session persistence for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute rules as described in [CFP-47089](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/102). Supported session persistence options are validated, with unsupported values being rejected. Accepted routes are ingested into the internal model and translated into CiliumEnvoyConfig. If a Gateway has any attached route rule containing a session persistence config, the Envoy stateful session filter is applied, alongside per-route cookie settings. Any routes attached to the Gateway without session persistence will explicitly disable the stateful session filter. The following HTTPRoute enables persistence for `/persistent`, while `/not-persistent` continues to use normal load balancing: ```yaml apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: name: example-route spec: parentRefs: - name: example-gateway rules: - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 sessionPersistence: type: Cookie sessionName: app-session cookieConfig: lifetimeType: Session - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /not-persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 ``` ```release-note Add support for Gateway API session persistence ``` AIL 2: Used to assist in planning, review, and generating some test cases.

signal.title: operator/ipam: Remove the per-node pool-maintainer retry trigger
signal.text: Each CiliumNode creates 4 triggers today, and one of them exists only to call another one: the "-retry" trigger's entire body is `poolMaintainer.Trigger()`, rate limited to one call per minute. That is one goroutine and one timer per node, which on a large enough production cluster where the majority of goroutine count is driven by node count, amounts to a quarter of the operator's parked trigger waiters. It exists only because of a skewed invariant. The two halves of `waitingForPoolMaintenance` live in different layers: the enqueue sites set it, and `MaintainIPPool` clears it on the one return path. Its early return for an unstable instances API returns with the flag still set, and the flag makes both `allocationNeeded()` and `releaseNeeded()` false, which gate the only two places that ever enqueue the maintainer. Nothing can re-drive the node, hence the retry trigger. This commit gives the flag a single owner instead. `MaintainIPPool` takes it on entry and releases it with a defer, so it is held for exactly the duration of a pass and released on every return path, and the enqueue sites only enqueue. The node reports its deficit again, so the interval based background resync re-drives it, and since that resync only reaches `Resync()` after a successful instances API resync, the node is picked up in the very iteration that observes the API recovering. While it is down the maintainer is re-triggered by node events rather than once per minute, but each of those is an early return that mutates nothing and is bounded by the backoff already applied to failed maintenance. This also fixes a latent strand on the second early return, taken while the instance has been stopped for less than a minute. Its comment says to wait for the custom resource to be updated as a sign of life, but that wait could never complete: `UpdatedResource()` marks the instance running and then consults `allocationNeeded()`, which was false because the flag was still set. A node that briefly stopped while in deficit stayed stranded until the operator restarted.

signal.title: mac: Make `mac.MAC` a `[6]byte`
signal.text: This PR migrates `pkg/mac.MAC` from being a [`net.HardwareAddr`](https://pkg.go.dev/net#HardwareAddr) (which is a `[]byte`) to being a `[6]byte`. Why we can do this: `net.HardwareAddr` has to be a slice because it has to support MAC address representations under different formats/size, such as the 20-octet IP over InfiniBand link-layer one. Cilium has always been stricter in the MAC addresses it accepts and already enforced the IEEE 802 MAC-48 format (see `mac.MAC`'s existing docstring: "MAC address is an net.HardwareAddr encapsulation to force cilium to only use MAC-48.") What we gain from doing this: We already wanted MAC-48-only format before, now this is guaranteed and enforced by the type itself, meaning we don't need to validate the value in as many places because once we have a valid `mac.MAC`, we know it's a 48 MAC. Switching from a slice to an array also means `MAC` becomes comparable (`m1 == m2`) and can be used as map keys (`map[mac.MAC]string` for example). From a memory point of view, an array is also better than a slice, but at this scale, the gain is probably not measurable. Overall, `[6]byte` is to `net.HardwareAddr` what `netip.Addr`/`netip.Prefix` are to `net.IP`/`net.IPNet`.

signal.title: Hide statedb table indexes behind query helpers
signal.text: Across several packages using statedb tables, the `statedb.Index` values were exported directly. This let callers depend on the index definitions rather than a stable query API. This PR unexports those index values in favor of small query helper functions (e.g. `NodeAddressByAddr`, `RouteByTableIndex`, `NeighborByIP`) that construct the query on the caller's behalf. This reduces the package API surface and keeps the underlying index implementation (name, key encoding, etc.) as an internal implementation detail that can't be depended on or modified by users of the package. AIL: 3. I instructed Claude to find candidate indexes to unexport and to suggest query helpers. I manually verified each replacement manually.

signal.title: Gateway API host-network: changing a listener port wedges Envoy in a permanent NACK loop that survives all restarts
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues Closest existing issues, both of which I think are distinct: - #45913 — TLS Passthrough listener on a non-standard port silently never binds. Same underlying listener-collapsing behaviour, different symptom (never binds, versus a permanent wedge after a change). - #34982 — one invalid listener stops updates for the others (closed as not planned, v1.16). Related to a secondary effect I hit, but it does not describe the persistence across restarts or the address-set cause. ## What happened? In Gateway API host-network mode, Cilium collapses every listener of a Gateway into a single Envoy listener whose address set carries all the ports (`additionalAddresses`). Changing any listener's port therefore changes that collapsed listener's **address set**, and Envoy cannot update a listener's addresses in place. It rejects the update: ``` error adding listener: 'kube-system/cilium-gateway-default/listener' has duplicate address '0.0.0.0:80,[::]:80,0.0.0.0:443,[::]:443' as existing listener ``` The rejection then becomes **permanent**. It survives restarting Envoy, restarting the agent, restarting both in either order, and restarting the operator. A fresh Envoy connects, binds the old ports, receives the current config, NACKs it, and retries every 15 seconds indefinitely. Deleting the `CiliumEnvoyConfig` does not help either: the operator regenerates it within seconds, so the agent appears to coalesce the delete and recreate into an update of the same resource name, and no removal ever reaches Envoy. ## What I think is going on My reading — and I would not be surprised to be wrong about the mechanism, since I inferred it from behaviour rather than from the source — is that the agent's xDS server replays the last **ACKed** version to each new Envoy stream before offering the current one. That would explain why a fresh Envoy binds the *old* ports before NACKing the new config, and why no amount of restarting escapes it: every new stream re-establishes the same stale state that caused the conflict. What I am confident about is the observable part: the address set changes, Envoy refuses the in-place update, and nothing short of removing the Gateway clears it. ## What does clear it Deleting the **Gateway** itself (not the CEC). The operator then tears the CEC down for real, the agent propagates an actual removal, and Envoy acks it — `lds: remove listener`, ports unbind, ack state clears. Re-applying the Gateway afterwards arrives as a clean ADD carrying the full address set, and every port binds first try in about ten seconds. Routes reattach by `parentRef` name, so deleting and recreating a same-named Gateway needs no route changes. The gateway serves nothing during the window, which was acceptable in my case only because the cutover already had the edge down. ## A related trap while diagnosing this `Gateway.status.listeners` reports `Programmed=True` for the whole duration of the wedge. That condition appears to reflect config generation rather than whether a socket exists, so every status signal looks healthy while nothing is bound. `netstat` on the node and an actual request were the only things that told the truth. If listener status could reflect the Envoy ACK state, this class of problem would be far easier to spot — though I appreciate that may be a larger change than it sounds. ## How to reproduce 1. Cilium with `gatewayAPI.enabled=true` and `gatewayAPI.hostNetwork.enabled=true` 2. A Gateway with an HTTP listener on `:80` and an HTTPS listener on `:443`, both bound and serving 3. Change one listener's port (in my case adding a listener that shifted the collapsed set) 4. Observe the agent log — `completing NACK` — and Envoy — `gRPC config ... rejected` 5. Restart Envoy, the agent, and the operator in any order; the NACK loop resumes each time 6. Delete the Gateway and re-apply it; everything binds immediately ## Cilium Version Observed on **1.20.0**. The cluster has since moved to 1.20.1 and I have not deliberately re-wedged it to confirm the behaviour is unchanged there, since it is now serving real traffic — so treat the 1.20.1 status as untested rather than fixed. ## Kernel Version Talos Linux v1.13.x, single-node cluster, one public IPv4. ## Kubernetes Version v1.36.x ## Regression Not known to be a regression — this was the first time I had used host-network mode, so I have no earlier version to compare against. ## Anything else? Two consequences I have written into my own runbook, in case they are useful for the docs: - Adding a listener on an **existing** port is safe, because the collapsed address set does not change — only the filter chains do. - Adding or changing a **port** is effectively a maintenance event rather than a config tweak, and should be planned like a restart. Happy to gather more detail, test a patch, or re-run the reproduction on a scratch cluster if that would help — I have the environment to hand.

signal.title: Host firewall: policy-selected node is permanently isolated after reboot — host endpoint policy map ends up deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip) or allow-all (runtime label add), never the computed policy
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? Closest match is #25448 ("host firewall drops reply traffic for legitimate connections when policies are first enforced"). This report is a stronger manifestation of what looks like the same enforcement-transition problem: in our setup the drop window is not transient — it is fatal and self-sustaining (node permanently isolated until out-of-band reboot), it reproduces on every cold boot, and it also reproduces on a fully synced agent when audit mode is switched off at runtime. Filing separately because the evidence points at the host endpoint's BPF policy map never receiving the computed allow entries, with three distinct end states depending on the path taken. ## What happened? Environment: Cilium 1.18.6 (kubespray), host firewall enabled, kube-proxy replacement enabled, VXLAN tunnel, WireGuard node encryption, `bpf-datapath-mode: netkit`, CRD identity mode, 61 nodes. A `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` with `nodeSelector` on worker nodes provides ingress lock-down (fromEntities cluster/remote-node/health/host, SSH/ICMP via CiliumCIDRGroup refs plus literal CIDRs, kubelet/NodePort from cluster). **1. Cold boot of a selected node → permanent isolation.** ~13 s after cilium-agent starts, every packet in and out is dropped as `Policy denied` by `bpf_host.c:865`. The node never recovers: the agent needs the apiserver to finish its sync, and its own egress to the apiserver is what is being dropped. Captured from inside a locked node (systemd unit dumping via crictl exec): - at agent start, `cilium-dbg endpoint list` is still **empty** (host endpoint not created yet) while bpf_host is already attached and enforcing deny-by-default with an empty policy map; - 105 659 `Policy denied` drops in 20 s, 73 018 of them the node's own egress to the apiserver LB: `identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:* -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443`; - at that moment the BPF ipcache is fully populated (8 292 entries) and local CIDR identities for the policy's allowed CIDRs are already allocated — e.g. ICMP from an explicitly allowed CIDR is dropped with its allocated identity (`identity 16777222->unknown`). The policy is computed; its allow entries are just not in the host endpoint policy map. **2. Runtime audit-off flip on a fully synced agent → same isolation.** Boot the node with `policy-audit-mode: true` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig): node comes up healthy, host endpoint reaches `state=ready`, realized policy has all 8 L4 ingress rules, `enforcement=audit-ingress`. Then `cilium-dbg endpoint config <hostep> PolicyAuditMode=Disabled` → "configuration updated successfully" → the node is fully isolated within seconds. The agent log ends abruptly mid incremental `UpdatePolicyMaps` processing with no error line — consistent with the deny default being installed while the allow entries never land. **3. Warm enforcement via label add → policy map silently allow-all.** With the agent fully synced and the node label added at runtime (CCNP starts selecting the node), the endpoint reports `enforcement=ingress`, but `cilium-dbg bpf policy get <hostep>` contains only the wildcard pair (`Allow Ingress ANY` prefix 0 / `Allow Egress ANY` prefix 0) — i.e. no actual enforcement. This is the only transition that leaves the node reachable, and it appears to do so by not programming the policy at all. For contrast, a long-running node whose agent processed the CCNP incrementally while already enforcing has a fully programmed map (per-identity allows, port ranges) — so the policy→map pipeline itself works. So the same policy, same version, produces three different host endpoint policy-map end states depending on the transition path: deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip), allow-all (runtime label add), correct (incremental update on an already-enforcing endpoint). Datapath mode does not appear to matter: a cold boot with `bpf-datapath-mode: veth` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig) locked out identically (caveat: the override's application could not be positively confirmed from inside the locked node). Impact: any reboot of a policy-selected node isolates it permanently; recovery requires out-of-band console/rescue access. 54 nodes affected in our cluster. ## Cilium Version 1.18.6 ## Kernel Version 6.8.0-124-generic (Ubuntu 24.04) ## Kubernetes Version v1.33.7 (kubespray) ## Sysdump Not attached (production cluster); can provide targeted captures on request. Full monitor drop capture (17 MB) and repeated boot-time snapshots of `endpoint list` / `bpf policy get` / `bpf ipcache list` from inside a locked node are preserved. ## Relevant log output ``` xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 7, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:39186 -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443 tcp SYN xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 2, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity 16777222->unknown: <allowed-admin-ip> -> <node-ip> icmp EchoRequest ``` Agent start with audit mode (the boot that survives): ``` level=warn msg="PolicyAuditMode is enabled. Network policy will not be enforced." level=info msg="Regenerating restored endpoints" restored=0 level=info msg="Creating host endpoint" ``` ## Anything else? - The reboot lockout window matches #25448's "first enforcement" semantics; unlike #25448 the state is permanent because the dropped traffic includes the agent's own apiserver path (chicken-and-egg). - Feature combination overlaps with #31209 (tunnel + KPR + WireGuard + host firewall). - Nothing relevant found in 1.18.7–1.18.13 changelogs. - Happy to run instrumented builds / additional captures on a dedicated test node. ## Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: NeighborDiscovery leaves stale forwardable-ip entries after node deletion

The node itself is no longer present, but the stale `forwardable-ip` owner keeps the neighbor entry alive. ## Expected behavior When the node is deleted, NeighborDiscovery should remove the node owner from the `forwardable-ip` table. If there are no remaining owners for the IP, the corresponding desired/kernel neighbor entry should eventually be removed as well. ## Actual behavior The deleted node remains as an owner of the `forwardable-ip` entry: ```text node:default/stage-jfpsf-wn5kt ``` and the kernel neighbor remains: ```text 10.23.35.70 dev eth0 managed extern_learn INCOMPLETE ``` or later: ```text 10.23.35.70 dev eth0 managed extern_learn FAILED ``` The stale neighbor is never cleaned up. ## Impact The stale neighbor causes repeated ARP resolution attempts for an IP that belongs to a deleted node. signal.title: gateway-api: an apiserver 500 during CRD discovery is treated as "CRDs not installed", disabling Gateway API for the lifetime of the operator
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? Follow-up to #43130 (fixed by #43452 and #44662). Those fixes handle the case where the apiserver is unreachable at the network level. This report is about the remaining hole: an apiserver that answers, but answers 500. `cilium-operator` started while etcd was going through a leader election. The Gateway API CRD discovery GET came back as a server-side error, the operator logged the "resources are not found" message and moved on with Gateway API off. No retry, no backoff warning, no restart. The pod then ran for two hours without a single further gateway-related log line, and the GatewayClass kept the default `Accepted=Unknown / Pending / "Waiting for controller"` status that the upstream CRD ships. Deleting the operator pod fixed it immediately. The CRDs were installed the whole time. The operator said they were not. Expected: a transient server-side failure is retried like a transient network failure, and if it does not clear, the operator exits so the kubelet restarts it. Only a real "the CRD is absent" answer should disable Gateway API silently. ### Mechanism `discoverCRDsWithRetry` splits every discovery failure into "retry" and "the CRDs are not installed" using `isTransientError`, and the second branch is the default: - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L162-L169 - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L365-L388 `isTransientError` is an allowlist: four `k8serrors` predicates (`IsServerTimeout`, `IsServiceUnavailable`, `IsTooManyRequests`, `IsTimeout`) plus four `syscall.Errno` values. A 500 carrying `Reason: InternalError` matches none of them, and that is exactly what the apiserver returns when the storage layer fails: `Internal error occurred: etcdserver: leader changed`. Neither does a bare 500 with no reason (`IsUnexpectedServerError`), nor a transport error that is not a plain `syscall.Errno`, such as `http2: client connection lost` or a `Client.Timeout` wrapped in `*url.Error`. Nothing upstream of that narrows it either. `checkCRDs` joins raw client errors, and `CheckCRD` returns the client error untouched; `NotFound` is never distinguished from anything else: - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/pkg/k8s/client/crd.go#L15-L37 So the branch that is supposed to mean "the operator looked and the CRD is genuinely absent" is reached by every failure mode the allowlist does not name, and its effect is permanent: `Enabled: false` is returned to the hive, `registerReconcilers` never runs, and no watch, timer or health probe re-enters the path. v1.19 is the same code, verified on the v1.19.7 tag: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/44d55ea770e38bdf4b3a5f5d8079ab311f5a4911/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L170-L177 ### Impact Any cluster where the control plane can return a server-side error for a second or two at operator startup. Managed and self-hosted control planes move etcd leadership during upgrades, node replacement and maintenance; the operator is restarted at exactly those moments. The failure is silent — the operator is Running and Ready, the message points at installation docs for CRDs that are already installed, and nothing recovers without a manual pod delete. ### Suggested fix Invert the default. Retry unless the error is specifically `k8serrors.IsNotFound`, i.e. treat "the CRD object does not exist" as the only permanent answer and everything else as retryable. That also removes the need to keep extending the allowlist for every new error shape. If the allowlist stays, it needs at least `IsInternalError` and `IsUnexpectedServerError`, plus a `net.Error` check for transport errors that do not carry an `Errno`. Either way the message on the permanent branch should be reworded: "resources are not found" is what sent me to check the CRDs first, and they were fine. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Install the Gateway API CRDs and enable `gatewayAPI.enabled=true`. 2. Make the apiserver return 500 for `GET /apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions/gatewayclasses.gateway.networking.k8s.io` for a few seconds during operator startup. Losing the etcd leader is the natural way; an admission webhook or a proxy that injects 500 works too. 3. Start `cilium-operator` into that window. 4. `kubectl get gatewayclass cilium -o yaml` stays at `Accepted=Unknown`, and the operator log has exactly one gateway line after the discovery message. It never recovers. ### Cilium Version v1.19.5 (vendored chart; behavior verified identical on the v1.19.7 tag) ### Kernel Version 6.18.38 (Talos v1.13.6) ### Kubernetes Version v1.35.6 ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell level=info msg="Checking for required and optional GatewayAPI resources" requiredGVK="[gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, Kind=gatewayclasses ...]" level=error msg="Required GatewayAPI resources are not found, please refer to docs for installation instructions" error="etcdserver: leader changed" The absence of the `"Failed to check GatewayAPI CRDs due to transient error, will retry"` warning is the tell: the backoff loop was never entered, the error went straight down the permanent branch on the first attempt. ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: bpf: Enable extended masquerade port range for BPF masquerade
signal.text: Under heavy outbound egress traffic, pods undergoing BPF masquerading can experience SNAT port exhaustion when restricted to the standard port range (`32768-65535`). This is a particular concern for users migrating from Kubernetes ip-masq-agent to Cilium eBPF masquerade, because the two have different default source port ranges: - Cilium eBPF masquerade selects any port in `32768-65535` by default. - Kubernetes ip-masq-agent selects any port in `1024-65535` by default. This change introduces support for configuring an extended masquerade port range (`--node-port-nat-range-ext`, e.g. `1024,29999`) across IPv4 and IPv6 to achieve source port range parity: 1. Refactor NAT Port Ranges into Runtime Config: - Replaced compile-time `#define NODEPORT_PORT_MIN/MAX_NAT` with dynamic BPF runtime config variables (`nodeport_port_min_nat` and `nodeport_port_max_nat`). 2. Extended Masquerade Port Range Support: - Added `--node-port-nat-range-ext` CLI flag in Hive loadbalancer configuration and mapped it to Helm. - Enforced validation rules (range bounds checking, ensuring non-overlap with NodePort range and privileged ports). - Implemented random port range selection in BPF for outgoing SNAT flows. - Added automatic fallback to the alternative range if the selected port range encounters allocation exhaustion. Fixes: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/23604 ```release-note bpf: Support configuring an extended masquerade port range (`--node-port-nat-range-ext`) for BPF SNAT masquerading. ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signal.title: pkg/idpool: lazy allocate idCache maps
signal.text: When `NewIDPool` creates an ID pool, it used to fill a map with every single ID right away. For a pool of 1,000,000 IDs, this took ~37.8 MB of memory and ~141 ms of setup time upfront before any IDs were even used. This change switches to allocating IDs on demand using a `nextID` counter. It only adds IDs to maps when they are released or inserted, saving memory and eliminating the setup delay. ### Benchmark Results - **Setup Time**: Reduced from **~141 ms** to **~33 ns** per operation. - **Memory Usage**: Reduced from **~37.8 MB** to **0 B** upfront allocation. - **Tests**: All unit tests pass; added `TestLazyIDPoolAllocation` and `BenchmarkNewIDPool`. signal.title: Split-Stage Deterministic NAT for egress gateway.
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? Current egress gateway implementation uses a single point of NAT node and faces the problem of single node scaling (can be solved using different gw for different targets), and redundancy problem as all gateways need synchronize their connection tables. Reling on a single egress gateway makes it harder to implement if the external traffic is so critical. Why we want to do this: - increase scalability using multiple active-active gateways. - minimal effect when switching between egress gateways. ### Describe the feature you'd like The solution or idea comes from [rfc6346](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6346) **Outbound, From POD to the related external traffic:** - Stage-1 : Node converts related extenal traffic onto the egress ip and port block calculated with deterministic CGNAT formula. It converts POD's ephemeral source port to an unsed port from the port block using conn track tables. It also changes the source port to the calculated egress ip. Then forwards traffic via tunnel to a egress gateway. - Stage-2 : Egress gateway accepts the packet and forwards it to the outside as source port and source address are already changed. **Inbound, From External to the POD (Response):** - Stage-2: Egress gateway looks at destination port and ip. It finds the responsible node from the deterministic CGNAT formula and then tunnels traffic to it. This gives ability to run multiple gateways. Return traffic can hit any of them and it will forward packet to the responsible node. - Stage-1: Node forwards the packet to the POD using conntrack table. ### Notify relevant community channels _No response_ ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution _No response_

signal.title: network driver: simplify statedb table management and remove redundant data from the table
signal.text: 1st commit fixes the text encoding/decoding for types.DeviceManager 2nd commit adds a merge method to the device - so we can preserve previously known attributes that did not show up in the more recent scan. for dummy devices this is no-op (no scanning takes place) but sr-iov devices may come in without a kernel interface name in the case the device is allocated to a pod (and therefore not visible in the root ns) 3rd commit includes: - removes attrs from statedb. these are only relevant when publishing resourceslices. produce these only when publishing. - publish step now ensures an allocated device retain the pool name it was allocated for. pool can only change between restarts/discovery events if the devices are not allocated - encapsulate row creation into a common function - use interface name instead of pool/interface name for the indexes - rewording some comments, dead code removal ```release-note network driver: simplify statedb table management and remove redundant data from the table ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signal.title: hubble: Add Kubernetes Pod UID to flow endpoints
signal.text: Hubble currently identifies a Pod mainly by cluster, namespace, and name. Kubernetes permits a deleted object's name to be reused, while its UID identifies that specific object lifetime. This matters especially for StatefulSet Pods, but applies to any recreated Pod. Adding the UID improves flow attribution. Consumers can distinguish Pod instances and correlate flows with Kubernetes records keyed by UID. The UID is carried through IPCache and ClusterMesh metadata, so Hubble can expose it for remote endpoints when that metadata is available. Local endpoints prefer the UID supplied by CNI and fall back to the Pod already attached to the endpoint when that UID is absent. Cilium also uses the UID internally: - IPCache deletion checks UID, preventing a delayed Pod, CEP, or CES deletion from removing metadata belonging to a replacement Pod. - Same-name Pod replacements update IPCache, cgroup, endpoint, and host-network state. IPCache and NOTRACK changes install new state before removing old state, allowing a short overlap instead of a gap. - Kubernetes drop events use the UID captured in the flow instead of resolving whichever Pod currently owns that namespace/name. The UID remains optional when metadata is unavailable or components are running mixed versions. This PR was prepared with AIL:4. Codex drafted the implementation and tests. I reviewed the code and changed the replacement handling. ```release-note Hubble flow endpoints now include the Kubernetes Pod UID. ```

signal.title: v1.19.3: WireGuard handshakes never complete on any node pair (tunnel/geneve + DSR), all cross-node pod traffic dead, on Oracle Linux only.
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? After upgrading to Cilium 1.19.3, all cross-node pod-to-pod connectivity is dead cluster-wide. The root symptom is that the WireGuard handshake never completes between *any* pair of nodes, in *either* direction. Every node reports, for every one of its 5 peers: ``` latest handshake: 0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z transfer: 0 B received, 9836672 B sent ``` ``` 96: cilium_wg0: <POINTOPOINT,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1300 ... RX: bytes packets errors dropped missed mcast 0 0 0 0 0 0 TX: bytes packets errors dropped carrier collsns 44358560 299720 0 2162782 0 0 ``` `cilium-dbg status` shows host connectivity is healthy while the encrypted overlay is completely dead: ``` Cluster health: 1/6 reachable (2026-07-28T13:02:11Z) cl-13-kubesi-worker-0: Host connectivity to 10.47.2.203: ICMP to stack: OK, RTT=297.168µs HTTP to agent: OK, RTT=961.602µs Endpoint connectivity to 10.42.2.197: ICMP to stack: Connection timed out HTTP to agent: Get "http://10.42.2.197:4240/hello": context deadline exceeded ``` With `echo module wireguard +p > /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control` on `controlplane-1`: (pattern repeats like this, no 'receiving' alike messages) ``` [427001.163104] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 11) [427001.163232] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Sending handshake initiation to peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) [427001.175653] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Sending handshake initiation to peer 1 (10.47.2.194:51871) [427004.235068] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 5 (10.47.3.11:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 2) [427006.284042] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 3 (10.47.2.217:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 12) [427006.284054] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 2 (10.47.2.203:51871) did not complete after 5 seconds, retrying (try 18) [427023.178883] wireguard: cilium_wg0: Handshake for peer 2 (10.47.2.203:51871) did not complete after 20 attempts, giving up ``` I ran claude on this, here's the output: ## What I have already ruled out I did a fairly deep investigation before filing. The following are all **not** the cause: | Hypothesis | Evidence against | |---|---| | **Public key mismatch** | All 6 nodes' live interface keys match their `CiliumNode` `network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key` annotations exactly, and match the corresponding peer entries on other nodes | | **Wrong endpoints / allowed-ips** | Each peer has `endpoint: <nodeIP>:51871` and `allowed ips: <nodeIP>/32`, which is correct for tunnel mode (geneve-encapsulated outer packet) | | **Clock skew (TAI64N replay rejection)** | Node clocks agree within ~1.8s | | **Cilium BPF dropping packets** | `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop -v` shows nothing during reproduction; `cilium-dbg bpf metrics list` shows no drop reasons other than an unrelated `Unsupported L3 protocol` on IPv6 RouterSolicitation | | **Issue #46100 (fragment tracking)** | No `DROP_FRAG_NOT_FOUND` counter present on any node. Handshake initiations are 148 B, far below any MTU | | **Host firewall** | `iptables` OUTPUT rule `ACCEPT all -- 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.0.0/8 state NEW` covers node-to-node traffic (2.7M packets); no DROP rule counter increments during reproduction | | **rp_filter** | `IPReversePathFilter` stays at 0 across bursts (note: `enp1s0/rp_filter=1`, `all=0`, so effective strict — but it is demonstrably not dropping these) | | **Network fabric blocking UDP** | Disproved by measurement — see below | | **Socket not bound / socket drops** | `ss -unlp` shows `UNCONN 0.0.0.0:51871`; `/proc/net/udp` shows `drops=0` for that socket | ### Measurement showing UDP does traverse the fabric Sending synthetic UDP bursts node-to-node (`worker-0` → `worker-1`, both `10.47.2.0/24`): - Receiver NIC counter (`/proc/net/dev`, counted before BPF): `5,603,727 → 5,608,812` = **+5,085 for 5,000 datagrams sent**. Packets reach the wire and the NIC. - Receiver netfilter INPUT hook, diffing `iptables-save -c` around a 3,000-packet burst to port 51871: ``` DELTA=3371 filter [27595:1956942] -A INPUT -m comment --comment "cilium-feeder: CILIUM_INPUT" -j CILIUM_INPUT DELTA=3361 filter [9070529:4141298931] -A INPUT -j KUBE-FIREWALL DELTA=3371 raw -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_raw DELTA=3371 mangle -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_mangle DELTA=2999 nat -A PREROUTING -j CILIUM_PRE_nat ``` So synthetic UDP to 51871 is routed for local delivery and passes netfilter without being dropped. Node-to-node TCP and ICMP work normally throughout (confirmed by Cilium's own health prober, RTT ~0.3–1 ms). So: the path carries UDP, the keys are right, nothing visibly drops the packets, and yet no peer ever answers a handshake initiation. ### How can we reproduce the issue? Surprisingly: this setup **works** on Ubuntu-based setup, I found this to be broken only on Oracle Linux 1. RKE2 cluster, 6 nodes (3 control-plane, 3 workers), Oracle Linux 9.8 / UEK kernel. 2. Cilium 1.19.3 with the config below: `routing-mode: tunnel` + `tunnel-protocol: geneve`, `encryption.type=wireguard` (nodeEncryption disabled), kube-proxy replacement with `loadBalancer.mode=dsr` and `dsrDispatch=geneve`. 3. Physical NIC MTU 9000 (happens on different clusters with "regular" MTU of 1500 too) , Cilium `MTU: 1380` (yields `cilium_wg0` MTU 1300). 4. Observe `cilium-dbg debuginfo | grep -A5 'peer:'`, all peers show `latest handshake: 0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` and `0 B received`. Relevant Helm values: ```yaml MTU: 1380 encryption: enabled: true type: wireguard tunnelProtocol: geneve kubeProxyReplacement: true loadBalancer: algorithm: maglev dsrDispatch: geneve mode: dsr bpf: masquerade: true hostLegacyRouting: false localRedirectPolicies: enabled: true pmtuDiscovery: enabled: true # or false, doesn't matter, both yield same outcome ``` ### Cilium Version `Cilium: Ok 1.19.3 (v1.19.3-f5eb641b)` ### Kernel Version ``` 5.15.0-322.203.3.4.el9uek.x86_64 ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` 1.35 (v1.35.5+rke2r2) [linux/amd64] ``` ### Regression Yes. This cluster worked before the upgrade to Cilium 1.19 (version: v1.18.3). Connectivity broke at the upgrade. WireGuard has never completed a single handshake in the current agents' lifetime (4d+ uptime, `latest handshake: never`). ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell KubeProxyReplacement: True [enp1s0 10.47.3.11 fe80::21a:4aff:fe16:1c4 10.47.17.1 (Direct Routing)] CNI Chaining: portmap Cilium: Ok 1.19.3 (v1.19.3-f5eb641b) IPAM: IPv4: 14/126 allocated from 10.42.0.128/25 Routing: Network: Tunnel [geneve] Host: BPF Attach Mode: Legacy TC Device Mode: veth Masquerading: BPF [enp1s0] 10.42.0.128/25 [IPv4: Enabled, IPv6: Disabled] Controller Status: 86/86 healthy Encryption: Wireguard [NodeEncryption: Disabled, cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: 7we7...fjk8=, Port: 51871, Peers: 5)] Cluster health: 1/6 reachable Modules Health: Stopped(23) Degraded(0) OK(113) ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: ipam/aws: Extract AWS-only logic from the global `pkg/ipam` package
signal.text: The goal of this PR is to introduce a clear separation between the generic IPAM machinery in `pkg/ipam` and the cloud provider specific integration (currently in `pkg/ipam/eni{,_test}.go`). There has always been some cloud specific bits and pieces under `pkg/ipam`, but this has significantly increased with the migration of ENI IPAM mode from the CRD IPAM allocator to the multi-pool IPAM allocator (https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/87). This PR is a preparation step to #46194: It introduces and defines a common shared interface that cloud provider integrations can implement. This will allow migrating both azure and alibabacloud to multipool without causing further proliferation of cloud-specific logic under `pkg/ipam`. As an added benefit, the new structure is fully hive-native, which will allow easily providing futher cloud-specific logic through hive (see https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47974#discussion_r3803867447). Note for reviewers: the first two commits should be easily reviewable as they are. For the third one, sadly the github UI does not detect well the moved code because of how the ~1600 lines of `pkg/ipam/eni{,_test}.go` are now split into smaller separate files under `pkg/aws/agent`. Most files are just moved code, the files you'll want to look at that are net-new code are `cell.go`, `doc.go` and `provider.go`.
signal.author: HadrienPatte

signal.title: operator/ipam: Restore fatal exit when the IPAM node watcher fails
signal.text: The cilium-nodes-watcher one-shot job bootstraps the cloud IPAM allocator, including the blocking initial synchronization with the cloud API. Before the switch to modular IPAM allocators, a failure there was fatal: `operator/cmd/root.go` called `logging.Fatal("Unable to start %s allocator")` and the operator exited, letting Kubernetes restart it. Moving that bootstrap into a `job.OneShot` dropped the fatality, as the job is registered without `job.WithShutdown()`. An unrecoverable failure is now only logged at error level by the job runner and marks the job degraded, leaving the operator running with no allocator and no node watcher: it can no longer hand out any IP, yet stays alive with no signal beyond a degraded health report. Add `job.WithShutdown()` to restore the previous behavior. The hive is shut down with the error, which `operator/cmd/root.go` turns into a single fatal log. Combined with the error chain repaired in f54b0828cb14 ("ipam: Return error from instance (re)sync instead of sentinel time.Time"), that log now also carries the underlying cloud API error, which the pre-regression fatal used to swallow. The `job.OneShot` runner returns early when the job succeeds or when the context is canceled, so a normal shutdown does not trigger this path. The node watcher is shared with the clusterpool and multipool allocators, which are equally unable to operate if their watcher fails to start, so they get the same treatment. Fixes: 9664b9b654c5 ("operator/ipam: Switch to modular IPAM allocators") Before (1.19): Currently (without this PR's fix, 1.20): (and after those logs, the operator pod sits idle forever, not logging anything else, instead of loudly crashing as we want it to) After this PR: And the operator ends up in CLBO as previously under 1.19

signal.title: node: Add NodeWriter and use it in NodeManager
signal.text: This introduces the `node.Writer` for controlled writes into the Table[Node]. On `Upsert` we check for conflicts with existing nodes. If a node exists with the same name, but different source then the highest priority source wins, and if a node exists with a different name that holds any of the addresses of the new node we check for source priority and if source is equal or higher the new node replaces the old node. As with NodeManager we don't set aside the losing nodes and restore them later. In other words, this aims to keep the same exact semantics as before. AIL:3 Related: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/41744

signal.title: gha: compute the ginkgo cache key once, before the matrix
signal.text: The E2E legs started failing with a template error before running any test: hashFiles('**/*.go') couldn't finish within 120 seconds, at line 445. hashFiles() runs on the runner under a 120s cap. The matrix jobs check out the trusted context ref at the root and the pull request branch under untrusted/, so the glob covers roughly 40k Go files instead of the 20k the tree has, and the walk competes with the LVH VM and the kind cluster that are already running. Hashing two trees also defeated the pre-build job, since the key saved over one tree never matched the key restored over two and every leg rebuilt the test binary that had just been built for it. Compute the key once in build-ginkgo-binary, where the tree is checked out once and the runner is idle, and hand it to the matrix as a job output. This commit was prepared with AIL:3.
signal.author: aanm

signal.title: cilium-cli: keep connectivity perf usable without Cilium
signal.text: The net-perf-gke baseline matrix job deliberately installs no Cilium: it runs cilium connectivity perf against a bare GKE cluster to produce the reference numbers the Cilium matrix jobs are compared against. Since ce7f9b264b, which detects the Cilium version in the perf setup path so the banner stops printing 0.0.0, that job fails within a second with "no cilium agent pods found in -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium", because initCiliumPods treats an empty pod list as fatal. Seen in https://github.com/cilium/cilium/actions/runs/32434777663 Let the perf setup tolerate a cluster with no agent. initCiliumPods now wraps a sentinel error for the empty case so the perf path can tell it apart from a failure to reach the Kubernetes API, which stays fatal, and version detection is skipped when there is no agent to ask. The Cilium matrix jobs are unaffected and keep reporting the real version. Verified in https://github.com/cilium/cilium/actions/runs/32474694911, where all seven matrix jobs passed. The baseline one logged "Skipping Cilium version detection: no cilium agent pods found in -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium" and then produced a full perf summary, while the native one still reported Cilium version 1.21.0. Fixes: ce7f9b264b ("cilium-cli/connectivity: detect Cilium version in connectivity perf setup") This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signal.title: BPF masquerading: Traffic to ExternalIP node addresses is masqueraded
signal.text: When using BPF masquerading, traffic to ExternalIP and InternalIP node addresses is not masqueraded by default. That was reported at https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/17177 previously and https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/37568 added a new flag, `enable-remote-node-masquerade`, to masquerade traffic to both ExternalIP and InternalIP node addresses. This isn't consistent with our iptables-based masquerading however. In that mode, we only masquerade traffic to ExternalIP addresses and assume traffic to InternalIP addresses is always routable. An additional optimization, making things consistent between the two modes, would distinguish ExternalIP and InternalIP addresses in the datapath to only masquerade traffic to ExternalIP addresses. We can probably achieve that via the node ID map.
